stories.title: Taoiseach to join Trump in Doonbeg on last day of visit
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump and Taoiseach Micheál Martin are to be reunited later today at the Irish Open golf tournament in Co Clare after President Trump prompted a diplomatic row yesterday when he backed a united Ireland. Speaking to reporters yesterday afternoon on the first day of his Irish trip, the US president claimed Irish reunification was inevitable, adding it "may as well happen now" - prompting pushback from British political leaders, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Mr Martin is to attend the final day of play at President Trump's golf resort in Doonbeg alongside other senior members of the Government, including Minister for Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media Patrick O'Donovan and Minister of State for Sport Charlie McConalogue. The trio are expected to feature when President Trump awards the trophy to the victorious golfer around teatime, which could be Offaly's Shane Lowry; he retired to the clubhouse yesterday evening with a four-shot lead. No formal meeting is scheduled between Mr Martin and President Trump, although the Fianna Fáil leader noted yesterday how Mr Trump had made similar comments about Irish unity over the past two years. President Trump could also traverse the course at some stage, having yesterday confined himself to a perch overlooking the 18th hole.

stories.title: Thousands turn out to protest Trump visit in Dublin
stories.summary: Thousands of protesters have gathered in Dublin amid one of the biggest policing operations in the history of the State for the visit of US President Donald Trump. At least 30 groups and political parties took part in the procession from Parnell Square to Dáil Éireann where a rally was held. Rolling road closures were in place during the march and there is a strong garda presence. People attending the march have spoke of their opposition to Mr Trump's visit and have criticised the welcome he has been given by the Government. Similar protests are taking place in Doonbeg in Co Clare where the US President is staying for the Irish Open. Mr Trump's visit began in Dublin and with that has come significant travel restrictions around Dublin Airport and Phoenix Park, which has since reopened.

stories.title: President voiced 'strong view' on war, genocide to Trump
stories.summary: President Catherine Connolly has said that she conveyed to the US president the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted. President Connolly and Donald Trump met for more than 20 minutes as part of a courtesy call at Áras an Uachtaráin this morning. The meeting in Phoenix Park did not have video cameras in the room but there were members of delegations present. Following a ceremonial welcome, including the signing of the Distinguished Visitors Book, the playing of the National Anthems, and the Inspection of a Guard of Honour, the two presidents met in the President’s Drawing Room. In a statement following the meeting, President Connolly said: "As President of Ireland, I am very conscious that Ireland and the United States of America are bound by strong ties. "This is a deep connection, built over centuries, which allows us to speak openly to one another.

stories.title: Oil falls but on track for 8% weekly gain on supply fears
stories.summary: Oil prices fell today but remained on course for a weekly gain of more than 8% while US diesel prices hit a record high as attacks along Middle East shipping routes stoked concerns about prolonged supply disruptions. Brent crude futures were down $2.68, or 2.5%, to $105 a barrel this evening, while US West Texas Intermediate crude fell $2.48, or 2.4%, to $100 a barrel. Both benchmarks hit their highest levels since mid-May earlier in the session. Both reversed early gains after the Financial Times reported that foreign ministers in the Middle East are trying to work out a temporary deal with Iran to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent and WTI rose more than 6% after an escalation in shipping attacks in the region yesterday. "Some headlines of possible new talks in the Middle East are weighing moderately on oil prices today," said UBS energy analyst Giovanni Staunovo. "I keep seeing near-term risks to the upside for oil prices, but we should expect ongoing high price volatility too."

stories.title: Saudis shut oil pipeline as Houthis tighten Red Sea grip
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline, after the vital oil conduit came under aerial attack in the widening Middle East war, threatening to send energy prices even higher. The world's largest crude oil exporter said it temporarily closed the pipeline as a precaution after a drone attack that both Baghdad and Riyadh said had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander in response to the attack. The 1,200km pipeline running across the Arabian Peninsula has served as the main route out for global supplies of Middle East oil for the past six months while the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shut by war. It has been moving 4-5 million barrels per day, amounting to 4% to 5% of global supply, sparing Saudi Arabia the brunt of the disruption that has crippled other Gulf oil and gas exporters. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the strikes.

stories.title: No credit in the bank for McGuinness after Kerry slaying
stories.summary: Would he or would he not? In the end, we found out this week that he would. Jim McGuinness has taken up the option of a fourth year in charge of Donegal, in this his second term as manager of the county's senior footballers. Perhaps it is no surprise, given that he will want to atone for how 2026 ended. In many ways Donegal's exit from the championship was somewhat bizarre on the year's longest day. The sun may have been at its highest overlooking Croke Park, but Donegal were deriving little energy from its rays despite taking Dublin to extra-time. It was clear to see that McGuinness's men were finding it a bit of a churn, though credit to them for forcing the additional periods after Michael Murphy nailed a late two-pointer. But it was just delaying the inevitable as the Dubs won with a bit to spare. The camera honed in on Murphy and the question of whether he'll grace the Jones's Road sod again was percolating. Still no word on the 37-year-old's Tír Chonaill future. After what Donegal had done for much of the previous six months, it may not be too hyperbolic to say that their championship exit bordered on the unbelievable - and we are not trying to go all Charlie Haughey GUBU here!

Emiliano Martinez then failed to deal with a corner and Belloumi drilled in via a deflection to put Sergej Jakirovic’s side on course for another upset at half-time. Chelsea tottered having again chucked away control of a match before their attacking prowess finally came to the fore once more to stave off an embarrassing home defeat. Cole Palmer was again their saviour. He found space to dig out a cross for Joao Pedro to rifle home midway through the second half and spare Alonso’s blushes.

stories.summary: Writer, director and composer Bobby Aherne introduces the new seaon below... If, like me, you've spent your life an avid imbiber of all forms of media, then the 'Geography’ section of your brain probably contains an entire atlas of places — largely islands — that don’t actually exist. From Gilligan’s Island to Yoshi’s one, isles Kirrin, Craggy, Monkey, Amity, Trash and Jurassic, and the rocks that hosted Truman Burbank, Mamma Mia! and McGoohan (debatably), we could probably navigate some nonexistent isles better than plenty of real places we’ve actually been to. Listen to the first episode of the latest series of Nero's Class Since yarn-spinners first started making stuff up, islands have proven to be the ideal setting for tall tales and fantastical fiction. See, islands can be whatever you want them to be: a blank canvas for the imagination, a self-contained microcosm of somewhere else, the perfect excuse to take your hero off-grid, and — in the case of somewhere like Summerisle — the most beautiful, picturesque, suffocating prison imaginable. In fiction, islands are almost always seen as a destination for some peace and quiet — two things that they rarely ever provide. I first became savvy to the poetic license provided by islands at some point in the mid-90s. After a family holiday to Inis Oírr, I took to writing a series of stories set somewhere called "Jeegara" — a far-away world made up entirely of 0-150 population islands with names like Jeesh Isle (named after my second class teacher’s favourite PG curse word), Gickile (home to Manure City and Fertiliser Bay), and The Grunki Scatter (your guess is as good as mine). Unfortunately, this creative streak happened to coincide with the opening of the Blanchardstown Centre just around the corner from my house — a development that sparked in me a simultaneous interest in liminal spaces, foreign franchises and mall mapping. In a confusing twist, this meant that all of my meticulously sketched, far-fetched fantasy lands ended up having their very own branches of Tuthills, Roches Stores, Smyths Toys and La Croissanterie. Capitalism had seeped into both the suburbs and my 9-year-old brain, which was seemingly only too eager to also help hoosh it out to a bunch of archipelagos in imaginary distant galaxies.

stories.title: Israeli-made Gaza documentary wins at Venice festival
stories.summary: A new documentary by two Israeli directors that accuses Israel of AI-assisted killing of civilians in Gaza won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday night. NAZA, by Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (No Other Land), had been tipped by some critics for the top Golden Lion prize for best film after a record-breaking 25-minute ovation at its premiere on Thursday. Receiving the award, Abraham said that in the 10 days since the festival began, "Israel killed six Palestinian children in Gaza at least." "The Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanisation of Palestinians," he told the audience. The Special Jury Prize is given out each year by the jury to recognise an outstanding work, but it is below the Golden and Silver Lions in order of merit. Abraham and Szor used conversations with 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who spoke on condition that their identities be protected.

This Irish Landmark Trust property dates back to the 1800s and is nestled on the edge of the Fota House estate. The nearby Fota arboretum and gardens is the perfect place for a brisk walk to spot the changing colours of the leaves. The house can sleep five people and is dog-friendly, making it perfect for friends or family groups. It has been beautifully designed and decorated by Jessie Wilkinson with wonderful pops of colour and plenty of snug areas to relax in the evenings.

stories.title: Demonstrations against Trump at Shannon Airport, Doonbeg
stories.summary: Protests have been staged at Shannon Airport and in Doonbeg, Co Clare, as US President Donald Trump arrived there this afternoon. Demonstrators in Doonbeg held placards and voiced their opposition to Mr Trump's foreign policies in what was a peaceful demonstration. Mr Trump arrived at his golf resort in the village shortly after 3pm aboard the Marine One helicopter. It circled the golf course, where the Irish Open is taking place, before landing, like Mr Trump had done on Air Force One earlier. A large crowd gathered near the tee box of the 17th to witness Marine One, two chinooks and another US helicopter land. Mr Trump was then taken in his armoured vehicle the short distance to the Trump International hotel where an armoured golf buggy awaited to take him around the golf course.

stories.summary: The cost of motor fuel on display at the service station down the road from where the Fine Gael parliamentary party met in Gorey in Wexford told the story starkly. The price of a litre of diesel was €2.03.9 with petrol not far behind on €1.92.9 this morning. This is the territory which sparked the fuel protests last April and prompted the Government to intervene. Back then it cut the cost of diesel by 32 cent per litre along with an excise reduction on petrol of 27 cent. That measure remains in place, and there were hints aplenty from the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris that it would not be phased out from November. He spoke about providing at least some degree of certainty on energy costs in the Budget, which is just 25 days away.

stories.title: Public sector workers threaten strike action next month
stories.summary: Public sector workers are planning to take strike action on two days next month if there is no progress on a new public sector pay deal. The Public Services Committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) met today and agreed that there would be work stoppages on 14 and 21 October. The committee is chaired by Fórsa General Secretary Kevin Callinan and, in an update to his members, he wrote that while several affiliate unions have concluded ballots and have a mandate for action, others are still in the process of completing balloting. "It was decided that unions would engage in strike action on Wednesday 14 October 2026 with pickets to be placed on workplaces," Mr Callinan wrote. In a video message to SIPTU local authority members, Divisional Organiser Brendan O'Brien said his division was issuing notice of industrial action commencing from 30 September. "In the event that that does not resolve the dispute, we will then escalate this dispute to two 24 hour stoppages, one of which will be on 14 October and the other will be on 21 October," he said.

stories.title: Lebanon's president pledges to achieve Israeli withdrawal
stories.summary: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has pledged to achieve an Israeli withdrawal and rebuild the area during a surprise visit to the country's south, after Israel captured and blew up a nearby Hezbollah position. Official Lebanese media said he arrived in the city of Nabatieh unannounced and accompanied by security officials including army chief Rodolphe Haykal. His visit comes a day after a senior US diplomatic official said a new round of US-brokered talks between Israel and Lebanon, initially scheduled for next week, had been pushed back to October. Mr Aoun expressed solidarity with locals in Nabatieh who greeted him, according to footage broadcast by Lebanese media. He praised staff at Nabatieh Governmental Hospital, saying they were risking their lives to provide medical services in the area, which most people have fled. Many government buildings and major sites have been destroyed in the city since fighting broke out between Israel and Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March.

stories.title: Kiely commits to Limerick for All-Ireland title defence
stories.summary: John Kiely will remain as Limerick senior hurling manager for their All-Ireland SHC title defence next year, with the county board confirming he's staying on "with the option to extend for a further season thereafter". He succeeded TJ Ryan back in September 2016, and went on to spectacularly revitalise Limerick's fortunes. Last July's defeat of Galway secured the sixth All-Ireland title of his rein. He's also won eight Munster crowns and four Allianz Hurling Leagues. "Limerick GAA can confirm that Limerick senior hurling manager John Kiely is to continue in his role for the 2027 season with an option to extend for a further season thereafter," a statement read. "The remainder of his management and backroom team will be confirmed in due course. The extension is subject to ratification by delegates at the October meeting of the Limerick County Board." Limerick GAA chairman Seamus McNamara added: "We are delighted that John is set to continue on in his role as Limerick senior hurling manager for at least another season. John, his management team and players have brought so much positivity to the county and we are delighted that he will remain at the helm for 2027."

stories.title: Nicole Flattery awarded 2026 Rooney Prize for Irish Literature
stories.summary: Nicole Flattery has been named the recipient of the 2026 Rooney Prize for Irish Literature at a gala dinner in Trinity College Dublin. The award, which marks its 50th anniversary this year, recognises an outstanding body of work by an emerging Irish writer under the age of 40. The annual prize has been doubled this year from €10,000 to €20,000 to mark the anniversary. The change was announced by the benefactor and custodian of the prize, Dr Peter Rooney. The oldest-established literary award in Ireland, The Rooney Prize is administered by the Oscar Wilde Centre for Creative Writing at Trinity College Dublin. Ms Flattery, originally from Kinnegad, Co Westmeath, was presented with the award at the event, which was attended by guests from the world of Irish literature, including 21 previous Rooney Prize winners. Previous recipients include Kate Cruise O'Brien (1979), Neil Jordan (1981), Frank McGuinness (1985), Glenn Patterson (1988), Anne Enright (1991), Colum McCann (1994), Mike McCormack (1996), Claire Keegan (2000), Claire Kilroy (2004), Kevin Barry (2007), Lucy Caldwell (2011), Doireann Ní Ghríofa (2016), Mark O’Connell (2019), Seán Hewitt (2022), Michael Magee (2023), and Suad Aldarra (2024).

stories.title: Danish drama Woman Unknown wins Venice Golden Lion
stories.summary: Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy's post-war drama Woman Unknown won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, with its star Mathilde Arcel also taking Best Actress honours in ⁠a rare double victory. El-Toukhy was the only woman to solely direct a feature film in the main 21-strong competition line-up, a disparity that drew criticism during the festival and prompted renewed scrutiny of the barriers facing women in cinema. Set in the aftermath of World War Two, Woman Unknown follows a housemaid played by Arcel whose past relationship with a German soldier threatens to destroy her future. The film unfolds against the backdrop of a newly liberated Denmark, where women accused of fraternising with occupying German forces were often subjected to vigilante justice. "To me personally, Woman Unknown is about the female body as a battleground and a public matter. And at the same time, the film tells the tale of women who are invisible, unseen, and voiceless," el-Toukhy said in her acceptance speech. stories.title: Trump visit is on par heading down the final fairway
stories.summary: A day of Dublin diplomacy for US President Donald Trump passed largely without drama, with the Irish Government spared his usual political fire. However, he turned the spotlight back on a united Ireland and delivered an awkward moment that became the focus for Irish and UK politicians. stories.title: Govt deliberately reversing Green policies - O'Gorman
stories.summary: Green leader Roderic O'Gorman has claimed the Government is trying to "ignore or deliberately reverse" a series of climate action policies introduced when his party was in power, despite repeated warnings of a growing climate crisis. Mr O'Gorman outlined his view at the start of its annual pre-Dáil think-in at the Ashling Hotel in Dublin. "Every step this Government has taken has been to either ignore or deliberately reverse measures we [the Green Party] took," he said. "Just yesterday it was announced that this summer was the hottest on record, and yet we have a Government which has actively tried to deconstruct the Climate Act, raided the Nature Fund, and, in September 2026, still hasn't been bothered to publish the Climate Action Plan for this year." Mr O'Gorman said that Minister for Climate and the Environment Darragh O'Brien "isn't even embarrassed about his foot-dragging on this [the Climate Action Plan] anymore, he's just built that in. "So time and time again the steps that could be taken to reduce emissions and make a meaningful impact are being ignored."

stories.title: UK economy grows at fastest pace since February 2025
stories.summary: The UK economy grew at the fastest annual pace in 18 months in July, helped by a boost from artificial intelligence and extending a strong first-half performance despite headwinds from the US-Iran war, official figures showed today. British gross domestic product in July was 1.6% higher than a year earlier, the fastest annual rate since February 2025 and above economists' 1.2% forecast, the Office for National Statistics figures showed today. The economy grew 0.4% on the month in July, compared with median expectations in a Reuters poll for output to be unchanged, and output in the three months to July - which smooths volatility - was also stronger than expected at 0.4%. Much of the growth over the past three months appeared to come from businesses involved in computer programming that were benefiting from the AI boom, the ONS' Director of Economic Statistics, Liz McKeown, said. "Looking at the latest month, services also drove growth in July, with computer programming again making the largest contribution," she added, noting an extra boost for some firms from the men's soccer World Cup and unusually hot weather. Sterling was little changed against the US dollar after the data and economists had mixed views about whether Britain's current economic outperformance would be sustained in the run-up to finance minister John Healey's first budget next month.

stories.title: West Bank sanctions a big moment in UK's foreign policy
stories.summary: It was forthright, it was clear, it was unequivocal - ethnic cleansing of Palestinians is being carried out in the West Bank by Israel. The formal position of the UK government now is that the occupation of the West Bank is illegal, and must end. It was a big moment in British foreign policy, and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's statement to the House of Commons was charged with emotion and freighted with history. "With permission, I would like to make a statement on Israel and Palestine," he said. "I do so as a proud British Jew, someone with the deepest gratitude to the state of Israel for giving a home to my grandmother after she lost her husband, my grandfather, and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis. "I remember visiting her in the 1970s in Tel Aviv and seeing the life and sanctuary Israel had provided. Indeed, some of my most joyful childhood memories are of picking oranges as a kid on the kibbutz where my cousins lived." This was how Mr Miliband began his speech laying out a major change in the tone and tenor of the UK’s relations with Israel. A speech his Israeli counterpart said "carries echoes of the antisemitic words" used by the former British military commander of mandatory Palestine in the interwar years.

stories.title: South Africa power past New Zealand to seal series win
stories.summary: South Africa scored four second-half tries as they powered to a 43-28 win over New Zealand in Baltimore to wrap up a 3-1 success in their Rugby's Greatest Rivalry Series. The world champions edged to a 17-14 lead at half-time before quickfire close-range tries from Malcolm Marx and Pieter-Steph du Toit swung the match their way. A Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty opened the scoring before All Blacks captain Codie Taylor crossed for an early try, Damian de Allende and Morne van den Berg responding before Will Jordan rounded off 32 phases with a try to cut the interval deficit. Ethan Blackadder pulled a try back after South Africa’s early second-half double, but as they pressed for another score, Kurt-Lee Arendse scooped up a loose ball deep in his own half and carved through a fragmented defence for an individual score. Cameron Hanekom seized on an All Blacks error near their own line to add a sixth try, Beauden Barrett crossing in the dying moments for a late consolation.
